item.title: The Alpha--Omega Problem in the Assessments of Atmospheric Power
item.description: arXiv:2610.38522v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Atmospheric power is commonly assessed with two Lorenz-cycle formulations treated as equivalent: the $\alpha\omega$ formulation, yielding gas expansion power $W_\omega$, and the $\mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla z$ formulation, yielding kinetic-energy generation by horizontal pressure gradients, $W_K$. We show that, for a statistically stationary global moist atmosphere, $W_\omega=W_K+W_P+W_{\rm nh}$, where $W_P$ is the power of lifting precipitating water and $W_{\rm nh}$ is power associated with departures from gas-phase hydrostatic balance. Since $W_P\simeq1$ W m$^{-2}$ globally, equality would require $W_{\rm nh}\simeq-W_P<0$, so the associated vertical force imbalance would have to do negative work globally. Using six-hourly ERA5, JRA-3Q, and MERRA-2 fields for 2025, we find that resolved $W_\omega$ varies by a factor of 1.7 (1.9--3.2 W m$^{-2}$), versus 1.2 for $W_K$ (2.4--2.8 W m$^{-2}$). Zonal-mean $\alpha\omega$ profiles have area-weighted contributions near $\pm50$ W m$^{-2}$, making global $W_\omega$ a cancellation residual, whereas $\mathbf{v}\cdot\nabla z$ profiles vary much less with latitude. The difference $W_\omega-W_K$ ranges from $-0.61$ to $+0.87$ W m$^{-2}$. Thus reanalysis-derived $W_\omega$ cannot provide an independent constraint on atmospheric power. Two treatments of the omitted surface layer give cross-reanalysis mean $W_K$ of 2.8 and 3.1 W m$^{-2}$, with corrected values spanning 2.6--3.5 W m$^{-2}$. Both exceed the observation-based Lorenz available-potential-energy generation estimate of 1.2 W m$^{-2}$. Assuming $W_{\rm nh}\geq0$, adding $W_P\simeq1$ W m$^{-2}$ gives total atmospheric power of about 3.8--4.1 W m$^{-2}$, motivating investigation of additional power-generation mechanisms.
item.dc:creator: Anastassia M. Makarieva, Andrei V. Nefiodov

item.title: SD3: The First Operationally-Proven, Fully Heterogeneous-Accelerated Global Kilometer-Scale Model with Inline Physics Architecture
item.description: arXiv:2610.39334v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present Super Dynamics on the Cube (SD3), the first operationally-proven, fully heterogeneous-accelerated global kilometer-scale model. Through a full-stack reconstruction in native CUDA C, SD3 introduces an "Inline Physics" architecture that deeply couples its non-hydrostatic cubed-sphere dynamical core with fast physical processes. This design maintains high physical consistency, ensures energy and mass conservation, and mitigates "Grey Zone" mismatches. Five years of continuous operational forecasting, together with validation against diverse observations, demonstrates the scientific fidelity of SD3. Recently, SD3 achieved an unprecedented 205.7 simulated days per day at global 1.5 km resolution using 24576 GPUs. SD3 establishes a hardware-agnostic, portable, and reproducible paradigm across diverse Exascale ecosystems. Beyond weather and climate research, SD3 offers a transformative paradigm for the HPC community and the next-generation Digital Twin Earth to establish a robust, high-performance blueprint for the future of Earth system modeling.
item.dc:creator: Yuan Liang, Xiaomin Hu, Xi Chen, Jingsheng Zhu, Li Yang, Leisheng Li, Qian Song, Xu Wang, Hao Wang, Zhenzhen Wang, Huiyuan Li

item.title: From extreme weather to agricultural consequences with agentic AI
item.description: arXiv:2610.40641v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Extreme weather is forecast days ahead, yet its consequences for agriculture remain hard to predict: a forecast says where a storm will strike, not which crops will suffer or how much is at risk, and the records that could tell span many sources. We present WxCrop, the first agent that judges agricultural hazards from physically interpretable weather indices examined by causal analysis, and the first that combines weather and agricultural information to predict crop loss reliably for past and forecast dates. We demonstrate it in Florida on hurricanes, freezes and dry heat, with a loss model calibrated on insurance records for each, and the same procedure extends to other hazards and areas. Three checks show reliability: the hurricane index detects recorded cyclone days with an AUC of 0.98, recorded losses in held-out years are reproduced to within 2%, and independent production records confirm the county rankings (rank correlation 0.63). Users ask the agent for each crop group's loss as a fraction of expected season value, every number sourced, so that governments, growers and scientists respond to agricultural disasters quickly.
item.dc:creator: Minghan Yu, Mengyu Dai, Yixin Wen, Haizhao Yang

item.title: Skillful and realistic precipitation forecasting with reinforced diffusion
item.description: arXiv:2610.38775v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Accurate precipitation forecasting remains elusive as physics-based models struggle to resolve mesoscale convection and machine learning often yields physically inconsistent, blurred results that consistently underestimate extreme events. We present FitzRoy, the first system that simultaneously achieves state-of-the-art predictive skill and physical realism over the continental United States. Through a reinforced diffusion framework, where a conditional discrete diffusion model is refined via reinforcement learning, FitzRoy effectively resolves the long-standing trade-off between pointwise accuracy and structural fidelity. Across lead times up to 24 hours, FitzRoy consistently matches or exceeds state-of-the-art models while preserving structural realism and capturing extreme events. Its low-latency inference further enables deployment in real-time operational settings. In case studies such as the 2025 Texas Hill Country floods and the 2026 Missouri floods, FitzRoy signals record-breaking accumulations that existing models largely missed. By bridging the gap between realism and skill, FitzRoy establishes a new frontier for high-fidelity precipitation forecasting.
item.dc:creator: Ozan Sener, Anand Avati, David Hafner, Jierui Lin, Laura Manduchi, Xiaoying Pang, Langwen Huang, Torsten Hoefler, Russ Schumacher, Vladlen Koltun

item.title: Critical-level wave absorption controls chaos in a wave--mean flow system
item.description: arXiv:2610.39809v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Wave-mean flow interactions in stratified fluids can drive spontaneous oscillations, yet the mechanisms controlling transitions between periodic and chaotic regimes remain poorly understood. Using a minimal one-dimensional model of wave-driven mean-flow reversals motivated by the quasi-biennial oscillation (QBO), we identify two distinct mechanisms that suppress the formation of multiple extrema in the velocity profile: critical-level momentum deposition by a broad spectrum of undamped small-scale gravity waves, and wave-amplitude growth due to exponential density stratification. Although physically distinct, both mechanisms inhibit the route to chaos and reduce sensitivity to small-scale viscosity, substantially widening the region of periodic behavior in parameter space. These results identify a general internal mechanism for the stabilization of wave-driven oscillations, with direct implications for QBO-like phenomena in geophysical and astrophysical flows.
item.dc:creator: Aymeric L\'evy-Dauchez, Louis-Philippe Nadeau, Antoine Venaille

item.title: Causal-prior-constrained deep learning for rapid-intensification warning of western North Pacific tropical cyclones
item.description: arXiv:2610.40304v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Rapid intensification (RI) is one of the most dangerous and unpredictable phases of tropical cyclones, and its environmental and structural drivers are difficult to identify and separate in observations. Here we introduce CausalVisionRI, a causal-prior-constrained deep-learning system for 24-h RI warning in the western North Pacific. It integrates infrared remote sensing imagery, atmospheric and oceanic fields, and an observationally discovered causal graph into a unified model. The graph and eight sign-verified effects on 24-h intensity change provide an auditable causal prior for training. Discovered from 522 cyclones in 2000-2017, it identifies causal pathways linking atmospheric and oceanic conditions, the cyclone's dynamical and structural state, and its 24-h intensity change. On a forward holdout covering 2020-2024 and 3,004 records, the five-member ensemble achieves a Brier skill score (BSS) of 0.259 relative to a fixed development climatology, significantly exceeding four reference systems; the three LDA baselines reach at most 0.105. It also attains higher detection rates than a published knowledge-block scheme and a reconstructed contrastive-learning scheme at matched false-detection rates under our USA 30-kt standard and the published RITCF standard. Ablations show that the graph pathway adds 0.032 BSS across the holdout and 0.063 over 2020-2021, with a significant contribution in one ensemble member. A deep-learning model constrained by observationally discovered causal structure thus offers a new route to physically informed RI warning.
item.dc:creator: Xinrui Li, Yijun Jin, Yifan Dong, Shoujuan Shu

item.title: Estimating the Kinetic Energy Spectrum from the Second-Order Velocity Structure Function using a Regularized Fitting Approach
item.description: arXiv:2604.27200v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ocean turbulence plays a key role in shaping large-scale circulation, heat uptake, and biogeochemical processes. The kinetic energy (KE) wavenumber spectrum is a fundamental diagnostic, quantifying how KE is distributed across spatial scales. The second-order structure function -- computed from velocity differences between spatially separated observations -- provides a complementary measure, but unlike the KE spectrum, it reflects a non-local, weighted integral of KE over all scales. Analytic relationships link the two metrics, permitting forward and inverse transformations between them. However, recovering the KE spectrum from the structure function via the inverse relationship is highly sensitive to sampling limitations and numerical discretization errors. Here we propose a regularized approach in which the spectrum is assumed to consist of a finite number of segments with distinct slopes and amplitudes, and the inversion is formulated as an optimization problem. The approach is first validated in an idealized setting; for a number of idealized KE spectra with prescribed sets of spectral slopes and amplitudes, the corresponding structure functions are computed by numerically evaluating the forward relationship. These structure functions are then used to determine the underlying parameters using our proposed approach, which shows that we are able to perfectly recover the parameters and consequently the KE spectra. The method is further evaluated on high-resolution ocean model output, where it reconstructs the underlying spectra well even in the presence of noise. Finally, we apply the method to surface drifter observations (GLAD and LASER experiments). The results show that the framework enables estimation of the KE spectrum from sparse Lagrangian data, extending spectral diagnostics beyond gridded Eulerian measurements.
item.dc:creator: Ayantika Bhattacharjee, Spencer Jones, Dhruv Balwada, Shane Elipot, Manuel Gutierrez-Villanueva

item.title: SwAIther-Precip: Lead-Time-Aware Bias Correction Enables Kilometer-Scale Downscaling of Global AI Precipitation Forecasts over Switzerland
item.description: arXiv:2605.16163v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Skillful medium-range precipitation forecasting at kilometer scale remains challenging over complex terrain because precipitation arises from multiscale nonlinear processes that global models cannot explicitly resolve at affordable cost. Global AI weather models can produce skillful medium-range forecasts, but their native 0.25 degrees resolution limits direct use for local hazard applications. Statistical downscaling can help bridge this gap, yet existing approaches often struggle with state-dependent, and especially lead-time-dependent, biases in global forecasts. We introduce SwAIther-Precip, a lead-time-aware downscaling framework that converts coarse-resolution AIFS forecasts into probabilistic km-scale precipitation fields over Switzerland. First, a U-Net conditioned on lead time via feature-wise linear modulation deterministically corrects systematic biases at coarse resolution. This targeted correction enables a cheaper super-resolution stage conditioned only on corrected precipitation, allowing direct training on observations rather than on the full atmospheric state. A diffusion-based model then generates fine-scale spatial variability independently of lead time. Using AIFS forecasts and CombiPrecip radar-gauge observations, SwAIther-Precip reduces CRPS by 48% relative to raw AIFS. The generated fields reproduce observed spatial variability with spectral fidelity above 0.85 at large scales and 0.88 at small scales, corresponding to an effective resolution of approximately 4 km on a 1 km grid for lead times up to 5 days. Training across lead times further improves long-range performance, yielding a 13% CRPS reduction at 6 days relative to lead-time-specific models. These results show that explicitly correcting lead-time-dependent biases before generative super-resolution is key to efficient km-scale probabilistic downscaling of global AI precipitation forecasts.
item.dc:creator: Dan Assouline, Erwan Koch, Federico Amato, Filippo Quarenghi, Daniele Nerini, Thibaut Loiseau, Kyle van de Langemheen, Tom Beucler

item.title: Wind vector retrieval from miniaturized wave-enabled sea-surface drifters
item.description: arXiv:2606.14520v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Open-ocean in situ winds are sparse, limiting the calibration and validation of satellite wind products. We evaluate wind-vector retrieval from MELODI (Miniaturized Electronics Lagrangian Oceanographic DrIfter), a compact freely drifting GNSS/IMU wave buoy. Wind speed is inferred from the shape of the measured wave acceleration spectrum. A regularized regression with a gated nonlinear correction (Wind Inversion using Tikhonov Regularization, WITR), trained on scatterometer winds and evaluated by leave-one-buoy-out cross-validation against ASCAT MetOp-B/C and HY-2B/C, gives a root-mean-square difference (RMSD) of 0.91 m/s. Symbolic regression distills the trained model into compact spectrum-only and motion-enhanced equations suitable for onboard use; the reduced drag law gives 0.93-0.94 m/s. Wind direction is estimated, without any fitted reference-wind regression, from IMU-derived directional wave moments in the 0.60-0.90 Hz wind-sea band, with a circular mean absolute angular difference (MAAD) of 9.4 degrees against ASCAT. These differences are comparable to published scatterometer-moored-buoy comparisons and improve substantially on the traditional single-band Toba inversion. Validation is strongest from 4 to 14 m/s and sparse above approximately 16 m/s; stronger winds are assigned low confidence. The results show that small wave-sensing drifters, calibrated to the well-established scatterometer wind scale, can provide useful wind-vector observations for validating satellite wind products and for atmospheric and wave modeling; stronger-wind sampling remains a priority.
item.dc:creator: Alexey S. Mironov

item.title: A common warming-dependent decline emerges from divergent projections of tropical cyclone frequency
item.description: arXiv:2609.16521v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: How global tropical cyclone frequency will respond to climate warming remains uncertain, with projections spanning both increases and decreases. Here we use an environment-dependent probabilistic tropical cyclone model driven by 14 CMIP6 models under intermediate- and high-emissions scenarios to identify a common response across these divergent projections. Initially weak global changes evolve into a clearer late-century decline, driven by increasingly negative changes in the Southern Hemisphere and diminishing positive changes in the Northern Hemisphere. The long-term decline is stronger under higher emissions. Counterfactual decomposition shows that this stronger decline cannot be explained by the sum of the individual predictor contributions, which largely offset one another, but is instead dominated by negative non-additive joint effects among absolute vorticity, vertical wind shear, relative humidity and potential intensity. Across 28 model-scenario projections, the global tropical cyclone frequency trend scales linearly with the level of global warming. Applying the fitted warming-frequency relationship at 2 degree C of warming relative to 1980-2014 narrows the 95% confidence interval for the projected frequency change from [-21.9%, +10.3%] to [-9.1%, -2.5%]. These results reconcile divergent projections through a common warming-dependent decline and identify the joint reorganization of large-scale environmental conditions as its primary driver.
item.dc:creator: Cong Gao, Ning Lin

item.title: FASST: A Compact Stateless Atmosphere Model for Long-Term Ocean Coupling
item.description: arXiv:2610.36297v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Coupled climate simulations are computationally expensive, largely because of the atmosphere. We introduce FASST, a coupled climate model that retains the prognostic POP2 ocean while replacing the atmosphere and sea ice with lightweight U-Net emulators. The atmospheric emulator is diagnostic, predicting surface fluxes from the evolving ocean-ice state every $6$ simulated hours, while the sea-ice emulator advances the ice state monthly. For $140$ years of unforced integration, FASST maintains a stable global-mean climate without SST restoring, with post-transient global-mean SST of $291.30 \pm 0.22\mathrm{K}$ compared with $291.25 \pm 0.10\mathrm{K}$ in CESM$2$ piControl. FASST also captures interannual Ni\~no-$3.4$ variability, although with weaker amplitude than CESM ($0.62\mathrm{K}$ versus $1.02\mathrm{K}$). These results demonstrate that a stateless learned atmosphere can sustain stable, free-running coupled climate simulations over century-scale integrations.
item.dc:creator: Pratham Aggarwal, Duncan Watson-Parris, William E. Chapman

item.title: Scale-aware and spatially-localised optimisation of kilometre-scale MLWP models
item.description: arXiv:2610.37325v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Preserving fine-scale structure without degrading spatial accuracy is a central challenge for kilometre-scale machine-learning weather prediction (MLWP). We introduce a loss based on the dual-tree complex wavelet transform that constrains atmospheric fields jointly by scale, location, and orientation. We evaluate its performance using an experimental joint global--regional FastNet configuration, which produces \SI{1.5}{km} forecasts over the UK alongside $\sim$\SI{31}{km} global forecasts. Relative to both mean-squared error (MSE) and an FFT-based spectral objective, the wavelet loss substantially improves spectral fidelity. Compared with MSE training, it maintains similar pointwise performance, improves neighbourhood-based verification, and produces sharper precipitation fields with more realistic intensity distributions. These results demonstrate that spatially localised wavelet constraints can preserve multiscale atmospheric structure while largely avoiding the loss of pointwise accuracy associated with globally supported spectral objectives.
item.dc:creator: James Chappell, Sophie Luise Arana, Jack Bowyer, Matthew Burnand, Alejandro Coca-Castro, Evangeline Corcoran, Eric G. Daub, Tom Dunstan, Noushin Eftekhari, Anna-Louise Ellis, J. item.title: On-ground calibration of the X-ray, gamma-ray, and relativistic electron detector onboard TARANIS
item.description: arXiv:2405.04836v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We developed the X-ray, Gamma-ray and Relativistic Electron detector (XGRE) onboard the TARANIS satellite, to investigate high-energy phenomena associated with lightning discharges such as terrestrial gamma-ray flashes and terrestrial electron beams. XGRE consisted of three sensors. Each sensor has one layer of LaBr$_{3}$ crystals for X-ray/gamma-ray detections, and two layers of plastic scintillators for electron and charged-particle discrimination. Since 2018, the flight model of XGRE was developed, and validation and calibration tests, such as a thermal cycle test and a calibration test with the sensors onboard the satellite were performed before the launch of TARANIS on 17 November 2020. The energy range of the LaBr$_{3}$ crystals sensitive to X-rays and gamma rays was determined to be 0.04-11.6 MeV, 0.08-11.0 MeV, and 0.08-11.3 MeV for XGRE1, 2, and 3, respectively. The energy resolution at 0.662 MeV (full width at half maximum) was to be 20.5%, 25.9%, and 28.6%, respectively. Results from the calibration test were then used to validate a simulation model of XGRE and TARANIS. By performing Monte Carlo simulations with the verified model, we calculated effective areas of XGRE to X-rays, gamma rays, electrons, and detector responses to incident photons and electrons coming from various elevation and azimuth angles.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Journal of Astronomical Telescopes, Instruments, and Systems 10(2), 026005 (7 May 2024)

item.title: The electrostatic-hydrodynamic interaction of two spheres in a linear compressional flow
item.description: arXiv:2512.24512v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We investigate the collision dynamics of two like-charged dielectric spheres in a uniaxial compressional flow, accounting for non-continuum lubrication interactions, van der Waals attraction, and the complete finite-dielectric electrostatic interaction. Mutual polarization causes the electrostatic force to behave substantially differently from the point-charge approximation and can produce strong near-field attraction despite far-field Coulomb repulsion, depending on the particle size and charge ratios. We identify a critical electrostatic strength above which particles approaching from the far field cannot reach contact. This threshold corresponds to a saddle-node bifurcation of the relative-trajectory field on the compressional axis. Below this threshold, near-field polarization-induced attraction can increase the upstream interception area and substantially enhance the collision efficiency. We report that electrostatic interactions lead to non-monotonic variations of collision efficiency with electrostatic strength, particle size ratio, and charge ratio. When electrostatic interactions remain repulsive at all separations, increasing their strength suppresses collisions monotonically. Non-continuum lubrication and van der Waals interactions further modify the collision efficiency, although sufficiently strong polarization-induced attraction can dominate these near-field effects. For weak electrostatic interactions, a perturbation analysis expresses the leading correction to the collision efficiency as a weighted average of the electrostatic force along the limiting colliding trajectory, with the weight concentrated in the lubrication region; this prediction agrees closely with the numerical results. These results demonstrate that finite-size polarization and near-field hydrodynamic interactions jointly govern the collision behaviour of like-charged particles in compressional flows.
item.dc:creator: Pijush Patra, Srikumar Warrier, Anubhab Roy

item.title: Instability of exact finite-amplitude acoustic-gravity waves
item.description:
arXiv:2610.35210v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Godin (	extit{J. Fluid Mech.}, vol. 767, 2015, pp. 52--64) showed that compressible fluids in a uniform gravity field support finite-amplitude incompressible wave motions, in which every parcel conserves pressure and density, and constructed exact Gerstner-type surface and edge waves, possibly carried by currents. Using the short-wavelength instability method for compressible flows, we show that these waves are linearly unstable above a critical steepness. The stability of each fluid level reduces to a Floquet problem depending on two parameters: the steepness $\mathfrak{e}=e^{ka_2}$ and $
u^2=(1-\mathfrak{e}^2)
u_0^2$, where $
u_0^2=\cos^2\alpha\,N_0^2/\Omega^2$, $N_0$ is the buoyancy frequency of the hydrostatic reference state, $\alpha$ the inclination of the plane of motion and $\Omega=(gk\cos\alpha)^{1/2}$ the intrinsic orbital frequency. In an isentropic fluid, a level is unstable if $\mathfrak{e}>1/3$, recovering Leblanc's threshold for Gerstner waves (	extit{J. Fluid Mech.}, vol. 506, 2004, pp. 245--254) and extending it to compressible surface and edge waves; weak stable stratification lowers the threshold to $ rac13- rac{32}{81}
u_0^2+O(
u_0^4)$. In an isothermal atmosphere, $
u_0^2=\kappa\cos\alpha/(kH)$, where $H$ is the pressure scale height. For horizontal wavelengths near $5.5\,H/\cos\alpha$, principal subharmonic resonance makes the critical steepness vanish. For the fast airglow wave observed by Hecht et al. (	extit{J. Geophys. Res.}, vol. 107, 2002, D20, 4444), which Godin interpreted with his solution, the lidar temperature places the layer in which this interpretation is consistent on this resonance, where the critical steepness is typically 0.1 instead of $1/3$. Instability is confined to a layer beneath the free surface of surface waves and to a wedge at the shoreline of edge waves.

item.title: Noise Steering: Exploiting Wake Steering and Acoustic Directivity for Noise-Constrained Wind Farm Control via Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.36888v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Existing noise mitigation strategies for wind farms usually consist in reducing turbines power output, without accounting for the wake interactions between them and the noise emission directivity. This leads to over-conservative policies and unexploited wind power. Yet, turbine yaw can simultaneously affect wake interactions and the direction of noise emission, offering an additional degree of freedom for farm-level noise control. We therefore propose Noise Steering, a model-free reinforcement learning (RL) strategy that jointly controls turbine yaw angles and power setpoints to maximise farm power while satisfying a local noise constraint in a defined region. To enable training at a reduced computational cost, a low-fidelity acoustic model is coupled with the steady-state FLORIS simulator. The RL agent effectively learns how to redirect wakes and noise directivity away from the protected region while redistributing power across the farm. On a six-turbine test farm, the policy satisfies the 40 dB noise constraint throughout the full range of turbulent winds, with an average power deficit of only 2% relative to greedy unimpeded control, and up to 7.7% at high wind speeds. In comparison, the industry-standard noise-reduced operation (NRO) baseline here generates an average power loss of 17%. When deployed in the higher-fidelity FASTFarm simulator, the policy largely retains its performance under steady and turbulent inflow, despite differences in simulation fidelity. These results demonstrate the potential of combining yaw control and power derating through RL to improve the power-noise trade-off in wind farm operation.
item.dc:creator: Mart\'in de Frutos, Baptiste Corban, Claire Bizon Monroc, Ana Bu\v{s}i\'c, Donatien Dubuc, Jiamin Zhud, Esteban Ferrer
